blocks.h: On completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

items.h: Describe the role of the actuary in a life insurance company and explain the obligations and professional standards of the statutory actuary under NIIRA 2025.

Explain the structure of a life table and define and use the key life table functions: lx (number living at age x), dx (deaths between age x and x+1), qx (probability of death), and px (probability of survival).

Describe the construction and sources of the principal mortality tables used in Nigerian life assurance practice, including the EFU Life Table, the OM92, and the A1967–70 tables, and explain the criteria for selecting the appropriate table for a given product.
Explain the objective of premium calculation in life insurance and derive the net premium for a simple term assurance and a pure endowment, using the present value of expected cash flows approach.
Explain the components of the gross premium, net premium plus expense loadings, and describe the three categories of expense: initial, renewal, and claims.

Define a policy reserve and explain why reserves are necessary in life insurance; describe the prospective and retrospective methods of reserve calculation and explain the circumstances in which each is used.

Describe the valuation basis for a life insurance portfolio, distinguish between best-estimate and prudent (loaded) valuation assumptions, and explain the concept of a solvency margin under the Risk-Based Capital framework introduced by NIIRA 2025.
Explain NIIRA 2025’s requirements for the mandatory annual actuarial valuation of a life insurer, the statutory actuary’s obligations, and the required NAICOM actuarial reporting.
Describe the three bonus systems used in participating (with-profit) life assurance in Nigeria (reversionary, terminal, and interim bonus) and explain how the bonus declaration process operates.
Explain the concepts of surrender value and paid-up value, describe the methods used to calculate them, and identify the NIIRA 2025 consumer protection obligations relating to their disclosure.

blocks.text: 13.1 Introduction: The Actuary’s Role in Life Insurance

blocks.h: Actuarial science is the mathematical and statistical discipline that quantifies financial risk over time. In life insurance, it is the foundation on which every product, every premium, every reserve, and every solvency assessment is built. The actuary translates the uncertain future (mortality rates, investment returns, policy lapses, expense inflation) into precise financial numbers that enable the insurer to price its products correctly, hold adequate reserves, and remain solvent across the full term of its long-dated obligations.

The relationship between actuarial science and life insurance is closer than in any other financial services sector. A bank lends money for defined periods and charges a fee; if the borrower defaults, the loss is current and containable. A life insurer commits to pay a defined sum at an uncertain future point, the death of the insured, which may be 30 or 40 years away. To price that commitment today, the insurer must make long-range assumptions about mortality, investment returns, and costs. The actuary is the professional responsible for those assumptions, and for the continuous monitoring of whether actual experience is consistent with them.

This chapter is addressed to insurance professionals who are not actuaries. Its purpose is not to train actuarial practitioners, that requires years of formal study, but to give underwriters, claims officers, product managers, compliance officers, and senior managers a confident working understanding of the actuarial concepts they encounter in their professional lives. The chapter covers the life table, premium calculation, reserves, valuation, bonus systems, and the NIIRA 2025 actuarial governance framework, with worked examples throughout.

blocks.text: 13.2 The Actuary’s Role and Professional Standards
13.2.1 Functions of the Life Insurance Actuary

blocks.h: The life insurance actuary performs the following core functions within the insurer’s organisational framework:

rows: Developing the actuarial pricing model for new and revised products; setting mortality, lapse, expense, and investment assumptions; conducting profit tests; advising on premium rates for NAICOM filing submissions.

Calculating the liabilities the insurer must hold in its statutory financial statements to meet all future policy obligations. This is the most fundamental actuarial function and is the basis of the annual actuarial valuation report.

Assessing whether the insurer holds sufficient capital above its liabilities to meet the RBC requirements under NIIRA 2025; conducting the Own Risk and Solvency Assessment (ORSA); stress-testing the balance sheet.
Designing the reinsurance programme; calculating appropriate retention limits; reviewing the actuarial consistency of reinsurance treaty terms with pricing assumptions.
Advising on the asset-liability matching strategy; ensuring the investment portfolio is consistent with the duration and currency profile of the policy liabilities.

Monitoring actual mortality, lapse, expense, and investment experience against pricing assumptions; reporting material deviations to management; recommending assumption updates when experience diverges persistently from expectations.
Calculating the actuarially supportable bonus declaration for participating policies; preparing the bonus recommendation report for Board approval.
Preparing the statutory actuarial valuation report and certificate required by NIIRA 2025; signing the actuarial certificate included in the insurer’s NAICOM returns.

blocks.h: NIIRA 2025 requires every life insurance company to appoint a Statutory Actuary, a Fellow of the Institute of Actuaries (FIA), the Faculty of Actuaries (FFA), the Society of Actuaries (FSA), the Casualty Actuarial Society, or another actuarial body recognised by NAICOM. The Statutory Actuary holds a specific statutory role distinct from any employee actuary on the insurer’s staff. Their primary obligations under NIIRA 2025 are:

items.h: To conduct an annual actuarial investigation of the financial condition of the insurer and certify the adequacy of its policy liabilities in the annual actuarial valuation report.

To sign the actuarial certificate appended to the insurer’s statutory accounts, confirming that the liabilities have been determined in accordance with sound actuarial principles and applicable regulatory requirements.
To advise the Board of Directors on the actuarial soundness of the insurer’s pricing, reserving, and capital strategy.

To report directly to NAICOM, independently of management, where the Statutory Actuary has formed the view that the insurer’s financial condition is materially deficient or that the Board has failed to act on material actuarial concerns.

blocks.h: This last obligation (the right and duty of the Statutory Actuary to report directly to the regulator) is a significant governance innovation introduced by NIIRA 2025. It reinforces the independence of the actuarial function from management and ensures that actuarial concerns cannot be suppressed by commercial or executive pressure.

blocks.text: 13.3 The Life Table and Mortality Functions
13.3.1 The Concept of the Life Table

blocks.h: A life table is a statistical table that tracks a hypothetical cohort of lives (conventionally 100,000 persons, called the radix) from a starting age (conventionally age 0) and records how many survive to each subsequent age as the cohort is progressively depleted by deaths. The life table is the foundational instrument of actuarial mortality analysis. It translates raw mortality data, the age-specific death rates observed in a population, into a structured mathematical framework from which the probability of survival and death at every age can be calculated.

The life table’s power for insurance purposes lies in what it enables: given that I know the probability of a 35-year-old dying before age 36, and the probability of a 36-year-old dying before age 37, and so on for every age, I can calculate the cost of insuring a 35-year-old’s life for any term, at any sum assured, under any premium payment structure. The entire edifice of life insurance pricing rests on this foundation.

blocks.text: 13.3.2 Key Life Table Functions: lx, dx, qx, and px

rows: The number of lives from the original cohort that are still alive at exact age x.
If l₀ = 100,000 (the starting cohort) and l₁ = 99,200, then 800 members of the cohort died between birth and age 1.
Deaths between age x and x+1
The number of lives that die between exact ages x and x+1. dx = lx − lx+1
If l₃₅ = 97,850 and l₃₆ = 97,570, then d₃₅ = 280: 280 members of the cohort died between age 35 and 36.
The probability that a life alive at exact age x will die before reaching age x+1. qx = dx / lx
If d₃₅ = 280 and l₃₅ = 97,850, then q₃₅ = 280 / 97,850 = 0.002861. A 35-year-old has a 0.29% chance of dying before their next birthday.
The probability that a life alive at exact age x will survive to age x+1. px = 1 − qx
If q₃₅ = 0.002861, then p₃₅ = 1 − 0.002861 = 0.997139. A 35-year-old has a 99.71% chance of surviving to age 36.

blocks.h: The relationship between these functions is exact and internally consistent. From any starting lx value, the full life table can be derived if the qx values are known at every age. Conversely, from the full lx column, all other functions can be calculated.

blocks.text: 13.3.3 Reading and Using the Life Table

blocks.title: Worked Example 13.1: Reading the EFU Life Table (Illustrative Values)

blocks.h: The following is an extract from an illustrative life table with values representative of Nigerian male mortality experience. (Note: exact EFU table values are actuarially derived; these illustrative values are presented for pedagogical clarity only.)

Observations: (1) qx increases with age, the probability of death rises from 0.25% at age 30 to 3.6% at age 65. (2) lx declines monotonically. (3) dx increases at older ages as the increasing qx applies to a declining but still substantial population.

blocks.title: Worked Example 13.2: Calculating the Probability of Surviving Multiple Years

blocks.h: Question: Using the table above, what is the probability that a life currently aged 40 will survive to age 45?
Solution: The probability that a life aged x survives to age x+n is denoted n px and is calculated as:
n px = lx+n ÷ lx
Therefore, the probability of a life aged 40 surviving to age 45 is:
5 p₄₀ = l₄₅ ÷ l₄₀ = 92,700 ÷ 95,300 = 0.9727
Interpretation: A 40-year-old has a 97.27% probability of surviving to age 45. The complement, 1 − 0.9727 = 0.0273, is the probability of dying between ages 40 and 45: a 2.73% chance.

blocks.text: 13.4.1 How a Mortality Table is Constructed

blocks.h: A mortality table is constructed from mortality experience data: the observation of deaths in a defined population over a defined period. The construction process involves:

items.h: Data collection: Deaths and exposures (person-years at risk) are recorded by age for the population under study, typically over a period of three to five years to ensure statistical credibility.

Crude mortality rate calculation: The crude (raw) mortality rate at each age is calculated as deaths divided by exposure. These rates are inherently volatile at extreme ages where the data volume is small.

Graduation (smoothing): Statistical graduation techniques are applied to smooth the crude rates into a consistent, monotonically increasing (at most ages) curve. A valid graduated mortality table has no implausible discontinuities between adjacent ages.

Projection (optional): Future mortality improvements may be projected using reduction factors or improvement scales. This is particularly relevant for annuity products where the insurer is exposed to longevity risk (the risk that policyholders live longer than expected).

blocks.h: The EFU Life Table (named after its original sponsoring entity) is the standard actuarial mortality table for Nigerian life insurance practice. It was developed from the combined mortality experience of Nigerian life insurance companies over a defined observation period, submitted to and compiled by the Institute of Actuaries of Nigeria (IAN). The EFU table provides:

items.h: Age- and sex-specific qx values for Nigerian insured lives, a population that is generally healthier and better-educated than the general Nigerian population (the insured population is positively self-selected).

Separate ultimate and select tables: the ultimate table gives mortality rates for the general insured population; select tables give lower rates for lives recently underwritten (who have been medically screened and have passed a health assessment).

Values that are generally lower than general population mortality rates (as published by the National Population Commission) because the insured population receives healthcare, is literate, and has the financial resources to purchase insurance.

blocks.h: The EFU table is the default basis for life assurance pricing, reserving, and valuation for individual Nigerian life products. Where an insurer has sufficient credible own-experience data, it may use a modified EFU basis or a blend of EFU and own-experience, subject to actuarial justification and NAICOM acceptance.

blocks.text: 13.4.3 International Mortality Tables: OM92 and A1967–70

blocks.h: Two international tables are referenced in Nigerian actuarial practice for specific product types or as benchmarks:

OM92 (and OF92 for females): Published by the UK Continuous Mortality Investigation Bureau, based on United Kingdom assured lives experience for the years surrounding 1992. The OM92 table reflects a well-measured, large-volume insured population with higher socioeconomic status and better healthcare access than the average Nigerian insured population. Nigerian actuaries use the OM92 as a reference benchmark and as the basis for certain group life and expatriate products, applying a loading factor (typically expressed as a percentage of the OM92 qx values) to adjust for the higher Nigerian mortality environment.

A1967–70: A UK annuity table based on annuitant mortality experience in the years 1967–70. Annuitants experience significantly lower mortality than assured lives of the same age, because annuity purchasers are self-selected for longevity (only those who expect to live long buy annuities). The A1967–70 table is used in Nigeria as a reference for annuity products, including the Retirement Life Annuity products regulated under the Pension Reform Act 2014. It is old by modern standards; most Nigerian actuaries project forward from this base using mortality improvement factors from global or sub-Saharan African studies.
The choice of mortality table for a given life insurance product is an actuarial decision that must be documented in the product’s pricing report. The guiding principles for table selection are:

items.h: The table should reflect the mortality experience of the population to which the product is being sold. A product targeting urban formal-sector employees in Lagos may use the EFU ultimate table; a product targeting rural agricultural workers may require a heavier (higher-mortality) basis.

The table should be consistent with the insurer’s own portfolio experience where that experience is statistically credible. Where the insurer’s claims experience consistently shows mortality 20% above the EFU table, pricing on the raw EFU table without a loading is an actuarial error.

For group life products, where the group membership is defined (e.g., employees of a specific company), the actuary may blend the standard table with the group’s own experience after a sufficient observation period.

NAICOM expects the mortality basis to be documented and defensible in the product filing report. Changing the mortality basis without updating the NAICOM filing constitutes a material product amendment requiring fresh approval.

blocks.text: 13.5.1 The Present Value of Expected Cash Flows

blocks.h: The fundamental principle of life insurance premium calculation is that the premium charged should equal the present value of the expected future benefits (and expenses), where ‘present value’ reflects both the time value of money (discounting) and the probability that each future payment will actually be required (mortality weighting).

In a fair actuarial basis, the insurer neither profits from nor subsidises the policyholder over the long term. The expected present value of premiums received equals the expected present value of benefits paid. This is the ‘equivalence principle’ and it is the starting point for every net premium calculation.
E[PV of Premiums] = E[PV of Benefits]

Where E[ ] denotes the expected value over all possible mortality outcomes for the life assured, and PV denotes present value using the pricing discount rate (investment return assumption). This equation is solved to find the premium, the single unknown, once benefits, term, discount rate, and mortality table are specified.

blocks.text: 13.5.2 Net Premium: The Pure Risk Component

blocks.h: The net premium is the portion of the total premium required purely to cover the expected cost of claims, with no loading for expenses. It is calculated directly from the mortality table and the assumed interest rate. Two standard products illustrate the approach:

blocks.title: Worked Example 13.3: Net Annual Premium: One-Year Term Assurance

blocks.h: A life insurer issues a one-year term assurance on a male aged 35, paying a death benefit of ₦500,000 if the assured dies within the year. The insurer’s mortality table gives q₃₅ = 0.002904. The insurer earns an investment return of 10% per annum on reserves held during the year.
Step 1: Expected claim cost in year 1 = Sum assured × qx = ₦500,000 × 0.002904 = ₦1,452
Step 2: Discount to present value. The claim, if it occurs, is paid at end of year. Discounted at 10%:
Net premium = ₦1,452 ÷ 1.10 = ₦1,320

Interpretation: The insurer must collect ₦1,320 from the policyholder at the start of the year (invested at 10% to yield ₦1,452 by year end) to meet the expected ₦1,452 expected claim cost. This is the net premium, the pure risk cost with no expense loading.

blocks.title: Worked Example 13.4: Extending to a Multi-Year Term Assurance

blocks.h: For a 5-year term assurance paying ₦1,000,000 on the death of a male aged 40 within 5 years, with a level annual premium paid at the start of each year (if alive), the net premium P is found by setting the expected present value of premiums equal to the expected present value of benefits.
Using the life table values and v = 1/1.10 (discount factor at 10%), the calculation proceeds as follows:

Expected PV of benefits = Sum of (probability of dying in each year) × (Sum assured) × (discount factor for that year). Expected PV of premiums = Sum of (probability of being alive at start of each year) × P × (discount factor for that year). Setting these equal and solving for P gives the level net annual premium. For the values in our illustrative table with a 10% interest rate and sum assured of ₦1,000,000, the net annual premium for a 40-year-old male is approximately ₦3,900 per annum. Note: This calculation involves the use of commutation functions (Dx, Cx, Mx) which are tabulated values derived from the life table and interest rate, widely used to streamline multi-year premium calculations.

blocks.text: 13.5.3 The Gross Premium: Adding Expense Loadings

blocks.h: In practice, the insurer must charge more than the net premium because the net premium covers only expected claims. The insurer also incurs:

rows: All costs of acquiring the policy: agent commission (first-year), medical examination fees, policy issue costs, proportion of head office overhead. Front-loaded; represent the largest expense item in year 1.
Expressed as a percentage of the sum assured or a fixed amount per policy. Added as a first-year loading; may be spread across the premium term using an amortisation factor.
Annual per-policy costs: premium collection, policy administration, annual statements, customer service. Incurred from year 2 onwards.
Expressed as a cost per policy per year or as a percentage of the annual premium. Added uniformly to each year’s premium.
The administrative cost of processing and settling claims when they occur.
Expressed as a fixed cost per claim. This is a relatively small component in most individual life products.
A loading above the ‘pure cost’ premium to provide a return on capital and a margin for adverse deviation in claims, lapses, or expenses.
Expressed as a percentage addition to the loaded premium. The size of this margin is determined by the profit test target IRR.

blocks.h: Gross Premium = Net Premium + Expense Loading + Profit Margin

In practice, the expense loading has a complex structure; it is not a single flat addition but a combination of a percentage of premium (to cover commission, which scales with premium size), a per-policy flat amount (to cover fixed administration costs), and a per-unit-of-sum-assured amount (to cover claims costs). The gross premium formula is solved for P in the same way as the net premium, by setting expected present value of gross premiums equal to expected present value of all outgoings (benefits + all expense items).

A life insurance policy creates an asymmetric cash flow profile for the insurer. In the early years of a long-term product (say, a 20-year endowment), the insurer collects premiums and incurs only initial expenses and a modest expected claims cost. In the later years, claims costs rise as the insured population ages and the maturity benefit approaches. If the insurer spent all early premiums on current expenses and surplus, it would have no funds to meet the larger obligations of later years. The policy reserve is the accumulation of these surplus early premiums, held as a liability to fund future policy obligations.

Reserves are therefore not an optional prudence measure; they are a mathematical necessity in any insurance product where the premium rate is level but the risk cost is age-progressive. This is the fundamental structural difference between life insurance and general insurance: general insurance is (mostly) one-year risk, repriced annually; life insurance is a multi-year commitment at a fixed premium, requiring systematic reserve accumulation.

The amount the insurer must hold in its balance sheet at any given duration to ensure it can meet all future obligations under the policy, assuming future experience develops in accordance with the valuation basis (mortality, interest, and expense assumptions). Also called the net premium reserve (when expenses are excluded from the calculation) or the gross premium reserve (when all expenses are included).

The prospective reserve is the most widely used reserve calculation method in life insurance. It defines the reserve at any duration t as the expected present value of future benefits less the expected present value of future premiums, both calculated using the valuation basis at duration t.
tV = EPV(Future Benefits) − EPV(Future Premiums)

Where tV is the reserve at duration t (t years after policy issue), and EPV denotes the expected present value using the valuation basis. If the EPV of future benefits exceeds the EPV of future premiums, the insurer holds a positive reserve (a liability). If, at inception (t = 0), the policy is priced on the same basis as the valuation basis, then 0V = 0 (the initial reserve is zero, the equivalence principle ensures this).

blocks.title: Worked Example 13.5: Prospective Reserve at Duration 5

blocks.h: A 10-year endowment policy on a life now aged 40 (policy issued at age 30) pays ₦5,000,000 on death or at maturity. At duration 5, the policyholder is now aged 35 and has 5 years remaining.

The prospective reserve at duration 5 = (EPV of paying ₦5,000,000 in 5 years, weighted by the probability the policy is still in force and either death or survival occurs) − (EPV of the remaining 5 annual premiums, weighted by the probability of surviving to pay each one).

Key principle: At duration 5, the reserve is always positive for an endowment because the 5 remaining premiums cannot cover the full expected cost of the maturity benefit and remaining death risk. The reserve represents the ‘savings component’ the insurer holds on the policyholder’s behalf.

Practical implication: If the policyholder surrenders at duration 5, the maximum surrender value the insurer can pay (without a loss) is approximately equal to the prospective reserve at that point, adjusted for the future renewal expenses that the insurer will save if the policy terminates. This is why surrender values are closely related to, but slightly below, the policy reserve.

The retrospective reserve defines the reserve at duration t as the accumulated value of the past surplus premium income, the excess of premiums received over claims and expenses paid, accumulated with investment returns to duration t. Under identical valuation assumptions, the prospective and retrospective methods give the same result; they are two different ways of computing the same quantity.
tV = AV(Past Premiums) − AV(Past Benefits and Expenses)

Where AV denotes accumulated value to duration t, using the valuation interest rate. The retrospective method is more intuitive for practitioners: it shows the reserve as the ‘savings account balance’ built up by the excess premiums. Its practical limitation is that it requires a complete record of all past cash flows, which makes it less useful for valuing large portfolios where historical records may be incomplete.

blocks.text: 13.6.4 Aggregate Reserves and the Valuation Report

blocks.h: The total policy reserve for the insurer’s entire in-force portfolio is the sum of individual policy reserves across all policies. The actuarial valuation calculates the reserve for every individual policy (or every homogeneous cell of policies in a seriatim valuation) and aggregates them into the total statutory liability reported in the insurer’s financial statements.

The relationship between reserves and the insurer’s financial position is direct: if the reserve is ₦50 billion and the insurer’s investment assets are ₦65 billion, the surplus (the excess of assets over liabilities) is ₦15 billion. This surplus represents the insurer’s capital buffer, the margin available to absorb adverse experience. NIIRA 2025’s Risk-Based Capital requirements specify the minimum surplus the insurer must maintain, expressed as a percentage of a risk-weighted measure of liabilities.

The valuation basis is the set of actuarial assumptions used to calculate policy reserves and assess the insurer’s financial position in the annual actuarial valuation. The valuation basis typically includes:

items.h: Mortality basis: The mortality table and any adjustments used to calculate the expected probability of death for each policy. The valuation mortality basis may differ from the pricing basis: the valuation basis is typically more prudent (heavier mortality) for life risk products and lighter for annuity products where longevity risk is the concern.

Interest rate (discount rate): The rate used to discount future expected cash flows to their present value. The valuation interest rate is typically set at or below the expected long-term portfolio yield, incorporating a prudence margin. It is the most sensitive assumption in the valuation: a 1% reduction in the valuation interest rate increases the reserve (liability) significantly for long-duration products.

Lapse and withdrawal basis: Assumptions about the rate at which policyholders will lapse, surrender, or convert to paid-up. For non-profit risk products, higher lapse rates tend to reduce reserves; for endowments and participating policies, lapse assumptions are more complex in their reserve impact.
Expense basis: The assumed future cost per policy of administering the in-force portfolio. For gross premium reserves (required under IFRS 17), full future expense assumptions must be modelled.

rows: Uses the actuary’s most likely expectation of future experience, the central scenario with no deliberate conservatism. Best-estimate assumptions include no margins for adverse deviation.
Used in: IFRS 17 financial reporting (Best Estimate of Liabilities, or BEL); management information and profit analysis; experience monitoring. NOT used for statutory solvency assessment.

Best-estimate assumptions plus a defined margin for adverse deviation. The prudent basis produces higher reserves (more conservative liabilities) than the best-estimate basis, providing a cushion against worse-than-expected experience.
Used in: NAICOM statutory valuation (the reserve figure in the annual actuarial report must be on a prudent basis); premium pricing (loaded assumptions in the gross premium calculation).

Extreme adverse assumptions used to test the insurer’s financial resilience under worst-case scenarios. Not used for central reserve calculation but for stress testing and RBC capital adequacy assessment.
Used in: ORSA stress tests under NIIRA 2025; scenario analysis in the actuarial valuation report; NAICOM supervisory stress tests.

blocks.text: 13.7.3 Risk-Based Capital and Solvency Margins under NIIRA 2025

blocks.h: NIIRA 2025 replaces the previous fixed-margin solvency requirement with a Risk-Based Capital (RBC) framework. Under RBC, the minimum capital requirement is not a fixed sum but a risk-sensitive amount that reflects the specific risk profile of each insurer’s portfolio.

The RBC framework requires the insurer to calculate a Total Risk Charge (the capital required to absorb unexpected adverse outcomes across all risk categories) and to hold capital (Total Available Capital) equal to or greater than this charge. The principal risk components of the Total Risk Charge for a Nigerian life insurer are:

items.h: Insurance Risk (C1): Capital required for adverse mortality, morbidity, and lapse experience relative to best-estimate assumptions.
Asset/Market Risk (C2): Capital required for adverse investment returns, credit defaults, and asset-liability duration mismatches.
Interest Rate Risk (C3): Capital required for interest rate movements that adversely affect the asset-liability matched position.
Operational Risk (C4): Capital required for operational failures, fraud, legal risk, and model risk.

blocks.h: Total Risk Charge = f(C1, C2, C3, C4) where f(·) is a combination formula specified by NAICOM that accounts for diversification between risk types.

Solvency Ratio = Total Available Capital ÷ Total Risk Charge. A solvency ratio ≥ 100% is the minimum threshold. NAICOM supervisory intervention is triggered at defined sub-100% thresholds. Insurers are expected to maintain a management buffer above the minimum.

Capital classification under NIIRA 2025: Tier 1 Capital (highest quality, paid-up ordinary shares, retained earnings, share premium); Tier 2 Capital (supplementary, revaluation reserves, subordinated debt with specified characteristics). NAICOM specifies the minimum proportion of Tier 1 Capital in the total.

NIIRA 2025 requires every life insurance company to commission an annual actuarial valuation of its total policy liabilities, to be completed within four months of the financial year end. The valuation must be conducted or approved by the Statutory Actuary. The Statutory Actuary’s report and certificate must be filed with NAICOM as part of the insurer’s annual regulatory return.
The mandatory contents of the actuarial valuation report under NIIRA 2025 include:

items.h: A description of the valuation basis (mortality, interest, lapse, and expense assumptions) and the justification for each assumption.
The total policy reserve by product category (individual life, group life, annuity, health), showing separately the reserve for participating and non-participating business.
An analysis of the change in the total reserve from the prior year valuation, decomposed by new business, claims paid, lapses, interest accretion, and assumption changes.

The Statutory Actuary’s professional opinion on the adequacy of the reserves, an unqualified opinion confirms that the reserves are adequate; a qualified opinion draws attention to specific areas of concern.
The RBC calculation and solvency ratio.
An actuarial experience investigation comparing actual mortality, lapse, and expense experience against the pricing and valuation assumptions, with commentary on material deviations.
For with-profit business: the recommended bonus declaration and the bonus declaration actuarial report.
A statement confirming that the underwriting guidelines and non-medical limits are consistent with the valuation mortality basis.

blocks.h: The International Financial Reporting Standard 17 (IFRS 17: Insurance Contracts) became effective for Nigerian insurers for reporting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2023, subject to NAICOM phasing provisions. IFRS 17 fundamentally changes the way life insurance liabilities are measured and reported in the financial statements.

Under IFRS 17, life insurance liabilities are measured on a current, market-consistent basis rather than the historically locked-in pricing basis used under the previous IFRS 4 standard. The IFRS 17 measurement model for life insurance contracts comprises three building blocks:

rows: Present Value of Future Cash Flows (PVFCF)
The probability-weighted present value of all future cash inflows (premiums) and outflows (claims, expenses, commissions), using current market-consistent discount rates.
Full actuarial cash flow model required; best-estimate assumptions for mortality, lapse, and expenses; market-consistent (risk-free or risk-adjusted) discount rates.
A quantification of the compensation the insurer requires for bearing the uncertainty in the timing and amount of future cash flows.
Calculated using a confidence interval or cost-of-capital approach. Represents the ‘prudence margin’ in IFRS 17 measurements. Requires actuarial judgement on the uncertainty in each assumption.
A deferred profit: the unearned portion of the profit locked in at contract inception. Released into income progressively over the coverage period as insurance services are provided.
Calculated at inception as the amount that, when added to the other building blocks, makes the total opening liability equal to the premium received. Released based on coverage units.

blocks.h: The actuarial function’s role in IFRS 17 compliance is substantial. The PVFCF calculation alone requires actuarial models of considerably greater granularity and data quality than the statutory valuation models previously used. Nigerian life insurers have been investing significantly in actuarial modelling infrastructure, data governance, and actuarial capacity to meet IFRS 17 requirements.

A participating (with-profit) policy is a life insurance product under which the policyholder is entitled to share in the distributable surplus (profits) generated by the with-profit fund. The fund’s surplus arises from three sources: favourable mortality experience (fewer deaths than expected); investment returns above the assumed rate; and expense savings below the assumed cost. The actuary’s role in the bonus process is to calculate how much of this surplus can be distributed as bonuses, consistent with maintaining the financial strength of the fund.

In Nigeria, with-profit products (particularly with-profit endowments and whole life policies) remain significant in the product portfolio, especially among older in-force business. New with-profit product issuance has declined as insurers have moved toward unit-linked and transparent savings structures, but the management of the existing with-profit fund represents a major actuarial governance responsibility.

A bonus added permanently to the sum assured of a participating policy at the end of each policy year, subject to the insurer’s annual bonus declaration. Once added, the reversionary bonus cannot be withdrawn by the insurer. It increases the guaranteed benefit (death benefit and/or maturity benefit) by a compound or simple accumulation of the declared annual rate. Reversionary bonuses are declared as a rate per ₦1,000 sum assured per year.

A participating whole life policy has a basic sum assured of ₦5,000,000. The insurer has declared reversionary bonuses of ₦25 per ₦1,000 sum assured per year for each of the last 10 years. (Simple bonus method: bonuses calculated on original sum assured each year.)
Annual bonus addition = (Sum Assured / 1,000) × Bonus rate
Total reversionary bonus after 10 years (simple method):
Total guaranteed death/maturity benefit after 10 years = Basic sum assured + Accumulated reversionary bonus = ₦5,000,000 + ₦1,250,000 = ₦6,250,000.

Under the compound bonus method, bonuses are calculated on the sum assured plus previously accrued bonuses (i.e., on the growing total), producing faster benefit accumulation than the simple method. The compound method is more policyholdholder-friendly but requires larger annual surplus distributions by the insurer to maintain.

A discretionary additional bonus, declared at the time a claim arises (death or maturity), over and above the accumulated reversionary bonuses. The terminal bonus is not guaranteed; it is declared at the insurer’s discretion at the point of claim, based on the accumulated surplus specifically attributable to the specific cohort of policies reaching that claim event at that time. Terminal bonuses can be substantial, particularly for long-duration policies in a period of strong investment performance.

Terminal bonuses reflect the fact that some of the investment surplus in the with-profit fund builds up over time and is most appropriately distributed at the point of claim. A reversionary bonus declared prematurely, before the full term of the policy, may lock in a surplus distribution that is not yet fully backed by realised investment returns. The terminal bonus provides a mechanism for the actuary to distribute accumulated unrealised gains (particularly property and equity appreciation) in a managed way at the point of exit.

From the policyholder’s perspective, the terminal bonus is valuable but uncertain; its amount is unknown during the policy term and can vary significantly between consecutive policy maturities if investment conditions change. Transparency in benefit illustrations is critical: NAICOM requires that terminal bonus projections in benefit illustrations be clearly identified as non-guaranteed.

A bonus paid on a claim (typically a death claim) that arises between the insurer’s annual bonus declaration dates. Because the reversionary bonus is declared annually, a policyholder who dies in the middle of a policy year has not received that year’s bonus. The interim bonus is an advance declaration of a proportionate share of the anticipated current-year bonus, paid on the claim to ensure the policyholder’s estate is not disadvantaged by the timing of death.

Interim bonuses are typically declared at the same rate as the most recent annual reversionary bonus declaration, applied pro-rata from the last policy anniversary to the date of death. They are a discretionary payment by the insurer, but their non-payment in circumstances where a bonus has already been earned by the fund’s recent performance would be a market conduct concern under NIIRA 2025’s treating customers fairly obligations.
The annual bonus declaration follows a defined actuarial process:

items.h: The actuary conducts the annual experience investigation and confirms the fund’s distributable surplus for the year.

The actuary models the impact of various bonus rate scenarios on the fund’s long-term financial strength, ensuring that the declared bonus does not deplete reserves to a level that threatens the security of future guaranteed benefits.
The actuary prepares a bonus recommendation report for the Board, setting out the recommended reversionary bonus rate, the proposed terminal bonus scale, and the rationale for each.

The Board approves (or modifies) the actuary’s recommendation. Boards have overridden actuarial recommendations on bonuses, typically to maintain a bonus in a difficult year for commercial reasons. This is acceptable provided the actuary’s professional opinion on financial sustainability is recorded in the minutes.
The approved bonus is declared and communicated to policyholders in the annual bonus statement.
The bonus is added to the policy reserve, increasing the insurer’s total liabilities and reducing the distributable surplus.

blocks.h: A surrender value is the cash amount the insurer pays to a policyholder who elects to terminate their policy before maturity by surrendering it to the insurer. The policy ceases upon surrender, and the policyholder receives the surrender value in full satisfaction of all future policy benefits.
The surrender value is calculated as an actuarially determined proportion of the policy reserve, with deductions for:

items.h: Unamortised acquisition costs: The initial expenses (agent commission, underwriting costs) incurred at policy issue have not yet been fully recovered from the premiums paid. In early policy years, the insurer makes a deduction from the reserve to recover the unrecovered portion of these front-loaded expenses.

Surrender charge (market value adjustment): Some products include an explicit surrender penalty in the first several years, expressed as a reducing scale (e.g., 10% of reserve in year 1, declining to nil by year 7). This incentivises policy persistency and compensates the insurer for the loss of the back-end margin that was assumed in the profit test.
Outstanding policy loans: The balance of any policy loan plus accrued interest is deducted from the surrender value before payment.

blocks.h: A 20-year endowment policy (basic sum assured ₦10,000,000) has been in force for 7 years. The actuarially calculated gross premium reserve at year 7 is ₦4,200,000. The policy’s surrender value table (per the policy document) specifies a year-7 surrender factor of 90% of reserve.
There is an outstanding policy loan of ₦480,000 (principal and accrued interest).
Calculation:
Gross Reserve:  ₦4,200,000
× Surrender Factor (90%):  ₦3,780,000
− Outstanding Loan:  ₦  480,000
= Surrender Value Payable: ₦3,300,000

Note: The policyholder paid premiums totalling approximately ₦3,500,000 over 7 years (7 × ₦500,000 annual premium). The surrender value of ₦3,300,000 is slightly below total premiums paid at this duration, reflecting the front-loaded expense recovery in the early years. By year 12–15, the surrender value would typically exceed total premiums paid as investment returns compound.

A paid-up policy is one where the policyholder has ceased premium payments before the original maturity date, but the policy remains in force for a reduced sum assured (the paid-up sum assured) with no further premium obligations. The policy continues to provide life cover until the original maturity date, but at a lower benefit level. If the policyholder dies before maturity, the paid-up sum assured (plus any accumulated bonuses on the paid-up policy) is paid; at maturity, the paid-up maturity benefit is paid.
Paid-Up Sum Assured = (Reserve at conversion) ÷ (EPV of ₦1 sum assured)

In practice, insurers calculate the paid-up sum assured as a proportion of the original sum assured: the proportion reflects how many premiums have been paid out of the total originally contracted. If 10 premiums have been paid out of 20 contracted, the paid-up value is approximately 50% of the original sum assured, adjusted for the time value of the reserve built up.

NIIRA 2025 Consumer Protection Obligations: The surrender value table and paid-up value basis must be included in the policy document in plain language. The policyholder must be notified proactively when a policy is at risk of lapsing due to unpaid premiums, and their right to convert to paid-up (rather than allowing the policy to lapse with no value) must be explicitly communicated. Failure to inform a policyholder of the paid-up conversion option before allowing their policy to lapse is a market conduct failure under NIIRA 2025.

blocks.text: 13.11 Advisory: Actuarial Communication for Non-Actuarial Professionals

blocks.h: One of the most important skills in a well-functioning life insurance company is the ability of actuaries to communicate complex quantitative concepts clearly to non-actuarial colleagues, and the ability of non-actuarial professionals to ask the right questions of their actuarial colleagues. This advisory section addresses both sides of that interface.

blocks.title: Advisory: Questions Every Senior Insurance Professional Should Be Able to Ask Their Actuary

blocks.h: The following questions test the actuarial health of a life insurance operation. Any senior manager, Board member, or regulator should be comfortable asking them, and should expect clear, quantified answers:

items.h: How does our actual mortality experience compare to the EFU table we are using for pricing? Are we over- or under-reserving relative to actual claims?

What is our current solvency ratio, and how does it change under the following stress scenarios: mortality 20% above pricing assumptions; investment returns 200 basis points below the valuation rate; lapse rates 50% above expected?
What is the sensitivity of our total reserve to a 1% change in the valuation interest rate? How large a movement in market rates would trigger a need for additional capital?

For our with-profit fund: is the current reversionary bonus rate sustainable over the next five years at current investment returns? What is the maximum bonus we can declare without reducing the terminal bonus reserve?
How many policies are currently in a paid-up state rather than in-force or lapsed? What is the aggregate paid-up liability and how is it reserved?
When was the last full actuarial experience investigation completed? What were the key findings? Which assumptions have been updated as a result?
What is the actuarial impact of IFRS 17 adoption on our reported surplus? Is the CSM growing, stable, or declining? What does that indicate about our new business profitability?

blocks.h: A professional trained in the mathematics and statistics of financial risk, specialising in the long-term financial implications of uncertain events. In life insurance, the actuary is responsible for pricing, reserving, capital assessment, and regulatory reporting.

The actuarially qualified professional appointed by a life insurance company under NIIRA 2025 who is responsible for the annual actuarial valuation and certificate, and who has a direct reporting obligation to NAICOM in cases of material financial concern.

A statistical table tracking a cohort of lives from a defined starting age, recording the number surviving to each subsequent age and the derived probability of death (qx) and survival (px) at each age.
A life table function: the number of lives from the original cohort (radix) that are still alive at exact age x.
A life table function: the number of lives dying between exact ages x and x+1. dx = lx − lx+1.
The probability that a life alive at exact age x will die before reaching age x+1. qx = dx / lx. The fundamental building block of all life insurance premium calculations.
The probability that a life alive at exact age x will survive to age x+1. px = 1 − qx.

The standard actuarial mortality table for Nigerian life insurance practice, derived from the experience of Nigerian insured lives. Provides age- and sex-specific qx values for individual pricing and reserving.

A United Kingdom mortality table based on assured lives experience around 1992. Used in Nigerian practice as a reference benchmark and for expatriate/group products, with appropriate adjustment factors for the Nigerian mortality environment.

The premium that exactly covers the expected cost of claims, with no loading for expenses or profit. Derived from the equivalence principle: expected present value of premiums equals expected present value of benefits.
The total premium charged to the policyholder, equal to the net premium plus loadings for initial expenses, renewal expenses, claims expenses, and profit margin.
The actuarial principle that the expected present value of premiums received must equal the expected present value of benefits paid. This principle determines the net premium.

The amount the insurer must hold in its balance sheet at any duration to meet all future policy obligations. Calculated by the prospective method (EPV of future benefits less EPV of future premiums) or the retrospective method.
The policy reserve calculated as the expected present value of future benefits minus the expected present value of future premiums, using the valuation basis.
The policy reserve calculated as the accumulated value of past premium income minus the accumulated value of past claims and expenses, using the valuation basis.
The set of actuarial assumptions (mortality table, interest rate, lapse rate, expense assumptions) used to calculate policy reserves in the annual actuarial valuation.
The capital adequacy framework introduced by NIIRA 2025 under which the minimum capital requirement is calculated as a risk-sensitive Total Risk Charge, rather than a fixed solvency margin.
Total Available Capital divided by Total Risk Charge under the RBC framework. A ratio of ≥ 100% is the minimum regulatory threshold.
A life insurance policy under which the policyholder is entitled to share in the distributable surplus of the with-profit fund, received as reversionary, terminal, or interim bonuses.
An annual bonus declared by the insurer and added permanently to the sum assured of a participating policy. Expressed as a rate per ₦1,000 sum assured per year.
A discretionary additional bonus paid at the point of claim (death or maturity), over and above accumulated reversionary bonuses. Not guaranteed.
A proportionate bonus paid on a death claim occurring between annual bonus declaration dates, representing the partial-year bonus earned up to the date of death.

The cash amount paid to a policyholder who elects to terminate their policy before maturity by surrendering it to the insurer. Calculated from the policy reserve, less a deduction for unamortised acquisition costs and surrender charges.

The reduced sum assured for which a policy is kept in force when the policyholder ceases premium payments before maturity. No further premiums are required; the policy continues until maturity at the lower benefit level.

International Financial Reporting Standard 17 (Insurance Contracts): the current IFRS standard governing the recognition, measurement, and presentation of insurance contract liabilities, requiring current market-consistent measurement of all life insurance liabilities.
Under IFRS 17, the deferred profit element of a life insurance contract liability, released into income progressively over the coverage period as insurance services are provided.

items.h: Dickson, D.C.M., Hardy, M.R., and Waters, H.R. Actuarial Mathematics for Life Contingent Risks (3rd edn, Cambridge University Press, 2020). The definitive graduate-level text for life contingencies. Chapters 4 and 5 cover the life table functions and present value calculations addressed in this chapter.

Bowers, N.L., Gerber, H.U., Hickman, J.C., Jones, D.A., and Nesbitt, C.J. Actuarial Mathematics (2nd edn, Society of Actuaries, 1997). Classic reference for life table functions, commutation functions, and premium calculation methodology.
Neill, A. Life Contingencies (Heinemann, 1977). A practitioner-oriented reference that remains useful for traditional life table approaches and commutation function application.

Institute and Faculty of Actuaries (IFoA). Subject CM1 (Actuarial Mathematics): Core Reading. ifoa.org.uk. The primary actuarial examination syllabus text for life contingencies; directly applicable to the mathematical content of this chapter.
Institute of Actuaries of Nigeria (IAN). EFU Nigerian Life Table: Technical Documentation. ian.org.ng.
Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act (NIIRA) 2025 (Act No. 2, 2025). Statutory Actuary provisions; mandatory annual actuarial valuation requirements; RBC framework. naicom.gov.ng.
NAICOM. Risk-Based Capital Framework: Guidelines for Nigerian Life Insurers. naicom.gov.ng.
Mondaq/Blackwoodstone. ‘The Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act 2025: Key Innovations and Business Implications.’ mondaq.com, November 2025. RBC and actuarial governance provisions.
Continuous Mortality Investigation (CMI), Institute and Faculty of Actuaries. OM92 (Assured Lives) and OF92 (Female Assured Lives) tables. Technical documentation available at cmi.org.uk.
Institute of Actuaries and Faculty of Actuaries. A1967–70 Annuitants Mortality Table. Used as reference for Nigerian annuity underwriting.
Institute and Faculty of Actuaries. CMI Mortality Projections Model (CMI Library). The standard tool for projecting future mortality improvement factors; referenced in annuity pricing for Nigeria.

International Accounting Standards Board (IASB). IFRS 17: Insurance Contracts. ifrs.org, May 2017 (effective 1 January 2023). The primary standard governing IFRS 17 measurement of life insurance liabilities.
Institute and Faculty of Actuaries. ‘IFRS 17: Practitioner’s Guide.’ ifoa.org.uk. Practical guidance on the actuarial implementation of the three building blocks.
PwC. ‘IFRS 17: A New Era for Insurance Accounting.’ pwc.com. Overview of IFRS 17’s impact on African insurance markets, with Nigeria-specific commentary.
Turnbull, C. A History of British Actuarial Thought (Springer, 2017). Chapter 8 addresses the development of with-profit (participating) life insurance and bonus systems.

Goford, J. ‘The Control Cycle: Financial Control of a Life Assurance Company.’ Journal of the Institute of Actuaries Students’ Society, 1985. A foundational paper on the management of the with-profit surplus.
